title: The Rooftop Messenger's Leap
markdown:
In Veridia the cobbles hummed forgotten tunes and the old rooftops played hide-and-seek with the clouds. Jun was a messenger, not a leaper. His satchel held vital missives, urgent pleas, and, on occasion, Aunt Mildred’s surprisingly robust rhubarb pie recipe. His talent was memory: every hidden alley, every dusty ledge, every shortcut that looked as if it belonged in a history book. His secret was simpler. Heights turned his knees to jelly. A second-storey balcony was enough.

Bea did not walk; she danced. The sky-high labyrinth was her kingdom. Pigeons were courtiers, stray cats sentinels, the wind a loud friend. She moved like a leaf that had decided to have opinions. She was the whirlwind to Jun’s careful anchor, the sparkle to his steady glow. Veridia would have been half as interesting without the pair of them, and twice as punctual.

One blazing afternoon Jun was delivering a dry decree about cheese tariffs to an official whose face suggested the cheese had already won, when a small unmarked envelope was pressed into his hand. The wax shimmered as if it had trapped starlight. No sender. No name. A prickle went over his skin. Monumental, the prickle said. His stomach did the flip that usually meant a detour and a late arrival.

He was about to tuck it into the inner pocket reserved for truly sensitive paper when a shadow fell.

“That message,” said a voice like gravel in a rusty can. “Give it here.”

Jun blinked. He was a messenger, not a drop-off. A tug on his sleeve: Bea, eyes bright, hair a wild halo.

“Running late, Jun? And who’s this grumpy badger who looks as if he’s misplaced a picnic?”

The shadow became a hulking man in a coat the colour of dried mud. A canyon of a frown. He glared at Bea, then at Jun.

“That message is not for delivery by you.”

His hand came out, not quite a blow, undeniably a demand.

“Oh, it isn’t?” Bea chirped. “Who decreed that? The Minister of Mean Faces? Did he send you for overdue smiles?”

The frown deepened. “Cease this foolishness. Hand over the letter before my patience wears thin.”

Jun, who usually froze at trouble, felt a spark. He clutched the envelope. He did not know why it mattered. He knew it did. Bea gave him a tiny nod.

“Looks like we’re off the usual postal route,” she whispered.

She grabbed his arm. “This way.” They went for the nearest stall, awnings flapping like startled moths. The man lunged. Boots hit cobble.

The Grand Bazaar took them in: cinnamon, saffron, something Jun could not name and would later try to. A woman selling copper pots laughed at a price and then at a better one. A boy balanced a tray of flatbreads as if the tray were a roof. Merchants in a dozen languages, a cheerful argument with the whole city. Jun, who knew the bazaar at ground level as a set of timed turns, discovered it had a vertical grammar. Bea stole them through a spice-stall’s shadow, apologised to a sack of cumin, and kept going. Their pursuer, lumbering, went out of tune with the joy and was swallowed for a minute by sleeves and spice. He reappeared by the fountain of the three fishes, too late, already a story the market would tell wrong.

“Up,” Bea shouted, pointing at a dizzying stack of crates.

Jun’s heart played a solo he had not auditioned for. He followed. He had to trust her. The thought of the drop made his knees bargain for a desk job. Bea’s hand on his back was an unexpected gravity.

Then the rooftops: sun-baked terracotta, clotheslines like tightropes, gargoyles that seemed to wink and then, on second look, not to. A cat watched them with professional interest and declined to help. Bea leaped chimney to chimney, a dancer who had hired the sky. Jun scrambled, stumbled, gasped. His satchel swung and he clamped it, thinking of Mildred’s recipe as a kind of ballast. Every gust felt personal. A gap between two houses showed a slice of street so far below it looked like a rumour.

“Next step,” Bea called, wind-clear. “Don’t look down. Forward. That blue tile. Aim.”

He tried. He saw her back against boundless blue. He chose a copper pipe’s glint, brick’s rough comfort under his palms. A sheet snapped on a line and he flinched as if it were a hand. Slowly, unbelievably, he moved. Not with her grace. He was moving. He put a boot where she had put a boot. He did not admire the view. He admired the next square of not-falling. He was running. He was running on rooftops, which was a sentence he had never expected to be true about himself.

They crossed a glasshouse roof that ticked in the heat. Bea went light. Jun went as if the glass were a letter he was not allowed to crease. Someone’s washing included a pair of trousers so large they might have been a sail; Bea used them as a screen and they dropped into a gutter run that smelled of old rain and thyme someone had planted in a chimney pot, which Jun filed as a fact for later, because messengers file everything.

Below, the pursuer became a frustrated silhouette, good at alleys and solid earth, lost at ballet.

Bea did not take them back to the street. She took them to a forgotten courtyard: ivy like a cloak, a fountain doing quiet work. Another century, pocketed in the noise. They collapsed on a mossy bench. Jun’s legs trembled. His chest heaved.

“That,” he panted, a shaky laugh, “was quite the delivery.”

Bea wiped dirt from her cheek. “Another day in the office. Now let’s see why people chase us like escaped canaries.”

Jun unsealed the wax. Elegant script. Still no name. A hidden heirloom, a family secret, a plea for safe return before the wrong hands closed. Those hands, they suspected, came with a muddy coat and friends.

“They must have seen me,” Jun said. “Known I’d be in the area. Known I might get this.”

A clatter at the courtyard mouth. Sparrows exploded upward. The first man stood there with two more, grim as librarians who had lost a first edition and blamed the weather.

“The letter,” he said, impatient. “It belongs to Lord Thorne. Immediate return. No complications.”

Jun, exhausted, almost handed it over. Then he remembered the plea in the script. He looked at Bea, steady, planted. He was no longer only an anxious postman. He had run. He had climbed. He had been in the story, not only beside it.

“Lord Thorne,” he said, and his voice held, “this letter speaks of a family heirloom sought for dubious reasons. It goes to its rightful guardian, not to someone who hounds messengers and ruins coats.”

The man scoffed, a rusty hinge. “Lord Thorne is the rightful guardian. He is a collector. He has precedence.”

Bea stepped in, gaze sharp. “A collector, or someone who takes what isn’t his? There’s a difference. It’s quite a large one, actually. You could put a chimney in it.”

Silence, except the fountain. Jun, emboldened, added, “This courtyard may be forgotten. The message isn’t. Perhaps Lord Thorne might try earning heirlooms instead of snatching them off the afternoon post.”

Another voice, clear and kind, came from the entrance. Calm arrived with it.

“Indeed. And I believe the rightful guardian is present.”

An elderly woman stepped in, face mapped with gentle wrinkles, eyes like forgotten stars. Simple elegant gown. Lavender. Jun and Bea looked at her, then at the muddy men, who seemed to shrink as if the courtyard had a setting for that.

The first man sputtered. “But Lord Thorne—”

“Lord Thorne,” she said, smile like a soft melody, “is a man of unconventional acquisition. This letter, young ones, is from my grandson. He asked me to find a courier with integrity. You, Jun, and your remarkable friend Bea, have proved more than capable.” The smile thinned for the men. “Perhaps you can explain your employer’s interest to the City Watch. I understand they are on their way.”

Panicked glances. A losing situation, especially with the Watch attached. A mumbled apology, an undignified retreat, a whiff of damp earth left behind like a poor review.

Jun and Bea watched them go. Exhilaration went between them without needing a stamp. Jun looked at his hands. They were not shaking. He had run the roofs, faced a grumpy collector’s dog, and spoken as if speech were a delivery he was allowed to make.

“You were incredible,” Bea said, nudging him. “I thought you’d float off. You kept going. A determined little mountain goat.”

Jun laughed, genuine, unburdened. “I couldn’t have done it without you. You showed me the way. You made me believe I could.” Warmth spread, a quiet confidence that had not been in the satchel that morning. The messenger who had feared heights more than a dragon’s hoard had found a use for ledges.

The old woman thanked them until gratitude became almost a second letter. She promised a reward that would make the satchel heavier with good fortune, and perhaps the rhubarb recipe in writing, which Jun considered a diplomatic triumph. As they walked the familiar streets, the city sat differently. Rooftops less of a threat. Alleys less of a plot. They had delivered more than parchment. They had delivered Jun to a version of himself that could look up without bargaining.

Bea stole a fig from a stall and paid for it, which she called character development. Jun checked the inner pocket from habit and found it empty of crisis. At the next corner a balcony leaned over the lane, second storey, the old enemy. He looked at it. His knees offered a mild opinion. He kept walking, satchel bumping, Bea already talking about a route across the tannery roofs that would cut six minutes off the cheese-tariff run, if he ever wanted it.

He did not say yes at once. He did not say no. In this line of work the best expeditions begin with a simple message and a step you have not practised. Sometimes the step is literal. Sometimes it is only the decision not to hand the letter to the first man who asks in a coat the colour of an argument.
